title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 154
paragraphs: Hearing this on his way, Cyrus said to Croesus as follows: “Croesus, what end shall I find of these things which are coming to pass? The Lydians, it seems, will not cease from giving me trouble and having trouble themselves. I wonder whether it were not best to sell them all as slaves; for I see that I have acted as if someone should slay the father and then spare his sons: just so I took you prisoner and am carrying you off, you who were much more than the father of the Lydians, while to the Lydians themselves I delivered up their city. And can I feel surprise, after this, that they have revolted from me?” Thus he said what was in his mind, but Croesus answered him as follows, fearing lest he destroy Sardis: “O king, what you have said is not without reason; but do not altogether give vent to your wrath, nor destroy an ancient city which is guiltless both of the former things and of those which have come to pass now. The former things I did, and I bear the consequences heaped upon my head; and as for what is now being done, since the wrongdoer is Pactyas, to whom you entrusted the charge of Sardis, let him pay the penalty. But pardon the Lydians, and lay upon them commands as follows, so that they may not revolt nor be a cause of danger to you: send to them and forbid them to possess weapons of war; bid them instead put on tunics under their outer garments and be shod with buskins; and proclaim to them that they are to train their sons to play the lyre and the harp and to be retail-dealers. Soon, O king, you shall see them become women instead of men, so that there will be no fear they will revolt from you.”
